_about.purpose: The complete legend of the Tunisia 1:50 000 series, transcribed row by row from the sheets, plus the analytic classes a dataset would be coded into. Two editions are printed in the series and a third group of sheets prints no legend at all.
_about.method: Read by eye at full scan resolution, in overlapping panels across the whole legend band. OCR was tried and is not adequate: Tesseract returns 'Chemin d'erploitation et sentier mulclier' for 'Chemin d'exploitation et sentier muletier'. OCR is used only to decide which edition a sheet carries - see scripts/read_sheet_legends.py.

_about.correction_note: An earlier version of this file, written from lower-resolution crops, recorded three differences between the editions that do not exist. Both editions name Oliviers and Palmiers in the Bois inset; both write the boundary row as 'de commune de plein exercice'; both write 'Ravine sans eau en ete'. Reading the legends at full resolution leaves only two real differences, listed under edition_differences.

edition_differences.1902: four maintained classes, named administratively: Route nationale; Route departementale; Chemin de grande communication et d'interet commun; Chemin vicinal ou autre chemin carrossable
edition_differences.1936: three maintained classes, named functionally: Route de grand parcours; Route de moyenne communication; Chemin vicinal
edition_differences.consequence: The two ladders are not the same scale with different labels; one has four rungs and the other three. Pooling them without a crosswalk mixes a legal classification with a traffic one. The four unmaintained classes below the brace are identical in both.
Same three glyphs, different word for the third. Note that 'Marabout' also appears in both editions in 'Clocher, Marabout: points trigonometriques', so the word alone does not identify an edition.

edition_differences.1902: not stated in the legend band on the Tunis sheet
edition_differences.1936: L'equidistance des courbes est de 10 metres, printed above the vegetation block
edition_differences.consequence: Contour interval is recoverable by script only on the later edition.

typographic_rule.note_on_sheet: Les ecritures droites designent les Villes, Bourgs, Villages, Hameaux, Fermes ou Usines et en general tous les lieux habites. Les ecritures penchees se rapportent aux Forets, Bois, Rivieres, Cols et Lieux-dits divers.
typographic_rule.meaning: Upright type is an inhabited place; sloped type is physical geography or a locality name. The map encodes the settlement/non-settlement distinction in the typeface itself - usable as a feature for OCR-based extraction, and a check on any classifier built from glyphs alone.

classes.symbol: small red circle (church) and a red bulb-on-stem glyph (koubba / marabout)
classes.research_note: The densest religious-geography layer available for the period. Marabouts that also carry the trigonometric glyph were used as survey stations, so their positions are control-quality rather than sketched.

classes.symbol: three distinct glyphs, one per confession
classes.research_note: The sheets type cemeteries by confession, in both editions. A mapped, pre-independence indicator of the confessional composition of a locality, with no counterpart in OSM or in any contemporary Tunisian dataset.

classes.symbol: small blue open circle (well); hooked blue glyph (fountain)
classes.research_note: Denser in the steppe and the south than any modern layer. Water access is the binding constraint on settlement in the interior.
Where irrigation exists it marks capital investment in the land, which is the north/interior gradient of interest.

Colonial coercive infrastructure, mappable against the civil settlement pattern. 'Poste optique' marks the optical-telegraph signalling chain across the interior, and is drawn on the map without appearing in the legend.

legend_row.1902: Limite d'Etat / de departement / d'arrondissement / de commune de plein exercice

classes.research_note: A four-level hierarchy, identically worded in both editions. 'Commune de plein exercice' is a status rather than just a unit: it names the settler-administered communes as against territory under other regimes.

legend_row.1902: four maintained classes plus four unmaintained
legend_row.1936: three maintained classes plus the same four unmaintained

classes.research_note: Ranked by construction and upkeep, so the class is a direct measure of state investment per kilometre. See edition_differences: the maintained ladder is not the same in the two editions and must not be pooled without a crosswalk.

classes.symbol: double dashed black line for roads; R.R. lettering for sites, which the legend does not define
classes.research_note: Marked exhaustively because the survey officers were looking for them. Useful as a proxy for antique settlement density and, with the henchirs, for long-run persistence questions.

legend_row.1902: Chemins de fer: a voie normale; a voie etroite et Tramway a vapeur; sur route; Passages en dessus / a niveau / en dessous

classes.research_note: Gauge is distinguished, and narrow gauge in Tunisia is largely the phosphate and ore network - an extraction geography rather than a passenger one. The specimen also names cuttings, embankments, tunnels, iron viaducts and stations, so the engineering works are individually drawn and countable as construction effort.

legend_row.1902: Bois (with Broussailles, Oliviers, Palmiers as named textures); Marais; Dunes et Sables; Vignes

classes.research_note: Olives, palms, scrub and woodland are separately textured in both editions, and vineyards have their own class. Vineyards approximate settler agriculture in this period; olives and palms are the indigenous tree economies of the Sahel and the Djerid.

legend_row.1902: Moulins a vent et a eau

classes.research_note: Rural processing capital, and the water mills locate perennial flow.
The clearest single marker of administrative presence in a locality, and a three-level ordinal rather than a binary.

legend_row.1902: Phare a feu fixe (portee en milles marins); Phare a eclipses; Feux de port

classes.research_note: Range in nautical miles is printed beside the glyph, so the class carries a numeric attribute.

legend_row.1902: Point trigonometrique; Clocher, Marabout: points trigonometriques

classes.research_note: Doubles as georeferencing control: these are the surveyed points the sheet was built on, and their heights are printed.

legend_row.1902: Passages de riviere: Pont en pierre, Pont suspendu avec piles, Passerelle, Bac, Gue (praticable aux voitures / pietons); Ravine sans eau en ete

classes.research_note: Crossing type is ranked by cost, from a stone bridge to a pedestrian ford, so river crossings are themselves an infrastructure-investment measure.

Outside the built-up areas, houses are drawn one by one in red. Counting them gives a settlement-density measure at a far finer grain than any place-name layer, and separates dispersed rural settlement from nucleated villages without classifying either.

legend_row.1936: L'equidistance des courbes est de 10 metres

classes.research_note: The interval is printed per sheet on the later edition and is read by scripts/read_sheet_margins.py; 10 m wherever it has been read.

classes._not_in_legend: The classes below are drawn on the sheets and named in the map body, but the legend does not admit they exist. They are the most valuable and the least discoverable.
classes.symbol: fine black dashed outline enclosing a named block of ground
classes.research_note: On the Sfax hinterland sheet the ground is divided into dashed-outline parcels, each labelled with a holding type and the lineage that holds it - a djenane (irrigated garden estate) or a henchir (large estate), followed by 'Oulad X'. Cadastral information printed on a topographic map, and the closest thing to a mapped land-tenure layer for the period. Parcel area is a distributional variable, so the boundary is worth extracting as geometry rather than as a label. Density varies sharply by region - dense around Sfax, absent on the steppe sheets - and that variation is a finding rather than a data defect.

classes.symbol: spaced capitals across open country; often prefixed 'Bled' or 'Melk'
classes.research_note: 'Bled X' names collective tribal land and 'Melk X' names private title; together the arch/melk tenure distinction that structures rural inequality in Tunisia. Printed as ordinary toponymy, so recoverable only by OCR plus a gazetteer.

legend_row.1902: Oliviers, a named texture in the Bois inset

classes.symbol: individual green hooked glyphs, one per tree or small group; distinct from the plain green stipple used for scrub
classes.research_note: The legend names the texture but not what it implies: the Sahel sheets draw olive trees individually rather than filling a polygon, so both the extent and the planting density of the groves are recoverable. Counting glyphs is template matching on a near-uniform mark, the easiest kind of symbol extraction on these sheets.

classes.symbol: red hatching for built-up area; type style distinguishes inhabited places
classes.research_note: The settler/indigenous distinction is drawn, not inferred: 'Village Francais' and 'Ferme Ecole' are labelled separately from the adjacent indigenous centre. 'Douar' and 'Henchir' are the rural units; a henchir is a ruined or held estate and often doubles as a land-tenure label. The legend offers no vocabulary for any of this beyond the typographic Nota.
